tier_reason: Peer-reviewed ASPLOS'22 paper (read in full; section 5) shows JSONSki beating simdjson (4.8x) and RapidJSON on end-to-end JSONPath time, and states G++ 7.4.0, -O3, 2x Xeon E5-2620 v4. It stays B, not A, because the repo holds only src/ and example/ with no baseline (RapidJSON/simdjson/Pison) harness, there is no artifact appendix, and baseline versions are unstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (single large record): "JSONSki runs over 12x faster over ... JPStream ... JSONSki is about 3x faster than Pison, and more than 4x faster than simdjson". ASPLOS'22 paper section 5.2: 12.3x over JPStream, 4.8x over simdjson, 3.1x over Pison on average (single large record, all single-threaded). README Fig.1 mean times: RapidJSON 5.07s, JPStream 4.90s, simdjson 1.92s, Pison 1.24s, JSONSki 0.40s, about 12.7x vs RapidJSON (derived from page data). README Fig.2 small records mean: RapidJSON 4.19s, simdjson 1.70s, JSONSki 0.41s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: G++ 7.4.0 with -O3 on CentOS 7 (ASPLOS'22 paper section 5.1); repo makefile builds with g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -mavx -mavx2 -msse -msse2 -msse4 -msse4.2 -mpclmul; README lists g++ 7.4.0 or higher as prerequisite
corrections.hardware: Two Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 @2.1GHz (16 cores), 128GB RAM, CentOS 7 (paper); requires 64-bit ALU, 256-bit SIMD (AVX2) and pclmulqdq
corrections.caveats: Baselines include parse/index time and use 2020-era simdjson/RapidJSON with versions unstated; no baseline harness is published in the repo, so the comparison is not reproducible from source. Paper notes single-threaded JSONSki is 48% slower than 16-thread speculative Pison on single large records. Only a JSONPath subset is supported (no '..', no filters); x86 AVX2+pclmul, Linux only; repo stale since 2024-10-10.

notes: README numbers match the paper's text (12.3x/4.8x/3.1x) and the README figure's mean bars. The dl.acm.org PDF returned 403 to curl and WebFetch, so the paper was read from the Wayback Machine copy of the same gold-OA ACM PDF. The Best Paper claim comes from the README and the author's page; the ASPLOS site was not checked.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 14(4) paper (read in full; section 6) shows end-to-end wins over RapidJSON (12.2X) and simdjson (4.6X), and states G++ 7.4.0, -O3, 2x Xeon E5-2620 v4. It stays B, not A, because the repo has no baseline harness (only src/ and example/) and baseline versions are unstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: "parallel Pison achieves 5.4X and 3.1X speedups (on average) over simdjson on Server 1 (with 8 threads) and Server 2 (with 4 threads)"; "both Pison and simdjson outperform RapidJSON"; serial Pison is "comparable to simdjson". README Fig.1 (Server 1) geo-mean end-to-end: RapidJSON 4.98s, simdjson 1.78s, Pison(1) 1.31s, Pison(8) 0.33s, about 15x vs RapidJSON (derived from page data). Peer-reviewed PVLDB'21 paper (section 6.4, Table 5, 16-core server): parallel Pison with 8 threads is 12.2X faster than RapidJSON and 4.6X faster than simdjson end-to-end.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: G++ 7.4.0 with -O3 on CentOS 7 (PVLDB'21 paper section 6.1); repo makefile builds with g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -mavx -mavx2 -msse -msse2 -msse4 -msse4.2 -mpclmul; README lists g++ 7.4.0 or higher as prerequisite
corrections.hardware: Server 1 (paper and README): 16-core, two Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 @2.1GHz, 64GB RAM, CentOS 7; Server 2 (README only): 4-core Intel Xeon E3-1240 v5 @3.5GHz, 16GB RAM
corrections.caveats: Headline win compares multithreaded Pison (8 or 4 threads) with single-threaded simdjson/RapidJSON. Serial Pison is about parity with simdjson (paper Table 5: sum 12.14s vs 11.9s, geo-mean 1.76s vs 1.93s). README 5.4X/3.1X numbers come from a different query set (one TT query vs the paper's TT1-TT8); the Server 2 results are not in the paper. simdjson/RapidJSON versions are unstated (2020 era); no baseline harness is published in the repo. x86 AVX2+pclmul, Linux only; repo stale since 2024-10-10.

notes: README figures confirm 5.4X (1.78/0.33) and 3.1X (0.78/0.25) vs simdjson. The peer-reviewed paper gives 4.6X vs simdjson and 12.2X vs RapidJSON, so B rests on the paper. The metric field says throughput, but the source measures end-to-end execution time. The metric field is outside the allowed corrections, so it was left unchanged.

tier_reason: nativejson-benchmark's only published results (sample/, 'Update on: 2016-9-9', clang 7.0 on Corei7-4980HQ) predate qajson4c's addition to the suite (PR #78 merged 2017-05-05) and contain no qajson4c row. The qajson4c README has only a qualitative claim with no numbers, so no numbers exist for this project.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No numbers found. README claims "Top scores at the nativejson-benchmark on category Parsing Memory, Parsing Memory Peak and AllocCount while scoring quite well at Parsing Time" (a memory claim, not a speed claim), but nativejson-benchmark's published sample results (2016-09-09) contain no qajson4c row.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 10 stars; wired into miloyip/nativejson-benchmark as a test target (submodule points to the fork USESystemEngineeringBV/qajson4c; PR #122 to repoint it to DeHecht/qajson4c is unmerged)
corrections.caveats: No published measurement exists: nativejson-benchmark's sample results predate qajson4c and the README gives no figures. Claim is about memory footprint and allocation count, not speed. Default branch last commit 2019-03-22 (branch iterative_parsing 2019-11-01); abandoned.

notes: Checked nativejson-benchmark sample CSV/HTML (mac64 and mac32) and conformance files: zero qajson4c matches. A third-party mmJSON benchmark (project-gemmi/benchmarking-json) also excludes it. Metadata is correct: MIT, not a fork, 10 stars, last default-branch commit 2019-03-22, abandoned.
